text: The Philistines gathered all their forces at Aphek, while Israel camped by the spring in Jezreel.
As the Philistine rulers marched past with their units of hundreds and thousands, David and his men came at the rear with Achish.

The Philistine commanders asked, "What are these Hebrews doing here?" Achish answered them, "This is David, the servant of Saul king of Israel. He has been with me now for days, even years, and from the day he deserted to me until now I have found no fault in him.

versions.text: The Philistine commanders asked, "What are these Hebrews doing here?" Achish answered them, "This is David, the servant of Saul king of Israel. He has been with me for a year or more, and from the day he deserted to me until now I have found no fault in him."
versions.explanation: The Hebrew reads "these days, or these years," an idiom for a considerable but unspecified length of time. "A year or more" fixes a period the text does not specify; a rendering that preserves the open-ended idiom is more accurate and reads well.

versions.text: He has been with me now for days, even years, and from the day he deserted to me until now I have found no fault in him.
versions.explanation: The first half of the verse is missing: the commanders' question about the Hebrews and Achish's identification of David as Saul's servant. Without it the verse begins with an unattributed "He" and the speech has no speaker. Restored from the earlier revision while keeping the intentional "for days, even years" idiom.

text: But the Philistine commanders were angry with him and said, "Send the man back. Let him return to the place you assigned him. He must not go into battle with us, or he will turn against us in the fighting. How better could he win back his master's favor than with the heads of these men of ours?"

versions.text: But the Philistine commanders were angry with him and said, "Send the man back. Let him return to the place you assigned him. He must not go into battle with us, or he will turn against us in the fighting. How better could he win back his master's favor than with the heads of our own men?
versions.explanation: The Hebrew has "those men" (i.e., the Philistine troops present). "Our own men" is a fair sense, but "these men of ours" stays closer to the demonstrative while keeping the rhetorical punch.

versions.text: How better could he win back his master's favor than with the heads of these men of ours?
versions.explanation: Nearly the whole verse is missing: the commanders' anger, the demand to send David back to his assigned place, and the warning that he must not go down to battle lest he become an adversary. Only the closing rhetorical question survives, leaving the speech without speaker or context. Restored from the earlier revision, keeping the intentional "these men of ours".

text: Isn't this the David they sang about in their dances: 'Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands'?"

So Achish called David and said to him, "As surely as the LORD lives, you have been honest, and it would please me to have you march out and back with me in the army, for I have found no wrong in you from the day you came to me until now. But the rulers do not approve of you.
Now go back, and go in peace; do nothing to displease the Philistine rulers."
"But what have I done?" David asked. "What have you found against your servant from the day I came to you until now, that I should not go and fight against the enemies of my lord the king?"
Achish answered, "I know you are as pleasing to me as an angel of God. But the Philistine commanders have said, 'He must not go up with us into battle.'

versions.text: Achish answered, "I know that in my eyes you are as good as an angel of God. But the Philistine commanders have said, 'He must not go up with us into battle.'
versions.explanation: "I know that in my eyes you are as good as" is clumsy for oral reading, stacking two qualifiers. "as pleasing to me as" carries טוֹב בְּעֵינַי naturally and flows better when read aloud.

text: So get up early in the morning, you and your master's servants who came with you; set out at daybreak, as soon as it is light, and go."
So David and his men got up early in the morning to return to the land of the Philistines, and the Philistines went up to Jezreel.
